Recorded on a quiet Apple M5 with

    go test -run xxx -bench . -benchtime 1x -benchmem

Another machine reads differently. What is committed here is the shape: an
order-of-magnitude move in any row means a refactor changed the complexity of
a path rather than its constant factor.

goos: darwin
goarch: arm64
pkg: github.com/maxxu123456/converge
cpu: Apple M5
BenchmarkSequentialTyping-10          	       1	 667639625 ns/op	5387209160 B/op	  900283 allocs/op
BenchmarkRemoteWhileTyping-10         	       1	  52230167 ns/op	82503392 B/op	  320079 allocs/op
BenchmarkRandomInsert-10              	       1	  48539208 ns/op	 8078512 B/op	   80054 allocs/op
BenchmarkSequentialDelete-10          	       1	  13920125 ns/op	56204480 B/op	   60004 allocs/op
BenchmarkLoadUpdate-10                	       1	   3141583 ns/op	  35.24 MB/s	 1509192 B/op	    3094 allocs/op
BenchmarkConcurrentMerge-10           	       1	   5181375 ns/op	 1679104 B/op	    6063 allocs/op
BenchmarkString1MB-10                 	       1	    292083 ns/op	3590.08 MB/s	 1056768 B/op	       1 allocs/op
BenchmarkEncodeStateAsUpdate1MB-10    	       1	   1754208 ns/op	 630.16 MB/s	 7627472 B/op	    2609 allocs/op

Two rows need reading notes.

SequentialTyping allocates 5.4 GB to type 100 000 runes. That is the design,
not a leak. Every keystroke folds into the run before it and copying a string
is the only way to grow one, so the bytes copied are quadratic in the length of
an unbroken typing burst. The time is not, because the copy is a memmove.
Anything that breaks the run (typing elsewhere, a remote insert, a delete)
resets the cost.

RemoteWhileTyping is the row that matters most. It is a tenth of the keystrokes
of SequentialTyping and should stay near a tenth of its time. If it goes
quadratic, the marker cache has started invalidating on a remote edit instead
of adjusting, and every correctness test still passes.
